objective: After this, a child in 7-10 can locate a place by following two compass clues (north, south, east, west) from a landmark already on the map, shown by a pin dropped within the round's tolerance.
why: A treasure map says: two steps east of the fountain, then one step north. Where is the treasure?
useElsewhere: Everyday life: giving a friend directions around school
Math: counting equal steps on a grid

objective: After this, a child in 7-10 can locate a place from a grid reference such as C-4, shown by tapping the correct square on a gridded map.
why: A treasure map says the chest is in square C-4. Without a way to name squares, you would have to describe it in a paragraph.
useElsewhere: Math: reading a coordinate grid (rows and columns)
Everyday life: finding a seat in a stadium or a street in an atlas index

objective: After this, a child in 10-18 can locate a place from its latitude and longitude, shown by a pin within the round's tolerance of the true point.
why: A ship's radio gives only two numbers for where it needs help. Which patch of ocean do you send the rescue boat to?
useElsewhere: Math: ordered pairs on a coordinate plane
Physics: locating a sound or signal source by two measurements

objective: After this, a child in 7-10 can sort six pictured places on a satellite map into mountains, plains, coast or desert, shown by correct placement of each card.
why: A new village needs flat land and fresh water close by. Where on the map would you build it, and where would you not?
useElsewhere: Physics: why rivers run downhill and rockfalls happen on steep slopes
Everyday life: choosing a safe place to build or camp

objective: After this, a child in 7-10 can estimate and compare the areas of two regions by counting grid squares in rows, shown by choosing the larger region and the number of squares.
why: Two farmers each claim the bigger field. Counting every square one at a time is slow; counting rows of equal squares is quick.
useElsewhere: Math: area as rows times columns (multiplication)
Economics: how many floor tiles or how much paint a room needs

objective: After this, a child in 10-18 can compare how crowded two regions are by dividing a count of people by an area, shown by choosing the more crowded region and giving the rate.
why: Town A has 1,000 people in 2 square km. Town B has 1,000 people in 8 square km. Which town is more crowded, and how do you know?
useElsewhere: Math: rates as division
Economics: price per item, cost per person
Chemistry: concentration as amount per volume (same idea, different setting)

objective: After this, an adult learner can explain why a flat world map makes regions near the poles look larger than they are, shown by ranking pairs of regions by true area against how big they appear.
why: On a common wall map Greenland looks about as large as Africa, which is far bigger. Plan a paint shipment by the picture and you order the wrong amount.
useElsewhere: Math: spheres versus flat sheets
Physics: why the same sunlight spreads over a bigger area near the poles

objective: After this, a child in 7-10 can find the distance between two places by counting how many scale-bar lengths fit along the route and multiplying, shown by entering the correct distance in whole units.
why: The class trip bus leaves at 9. The teacher wants to know how far it is from school to the museum, and the map only shows a little bar marked "10 km".
useElsewhere: Math: equal groups, skip counting, multiplication
Everyday life: how many blocks to the shop at 100 m each

objective: After this, a child in 7-10 can work out how many whole hours a trip takes when the bus covers the same distance each hour, shown by choosing the correct arrival time on a clock.

standard.source: Fragment of the standard's opening seen in a published alignment document (https://www.firstinspires.org/hubfs/Education_Resources/standards-alignment/fll-challenge/fll-challenge-alignments-CC-Math.pdf). Full text not fetched from corestandards.org (404 on 2026-11-10). Confidence MEDIUM.

why: The bus drives 40 km every hour and the museum is 120 km away. Will you be back before the lunch bell?
useElsewhere: Math: division as sharing 120 into groups of 40
Physics: later, speed = distance divided by time
Everyday life: planning when to leave for a match

objective: After this, a child in 10-18 can convert a length measured on a map to a real distance using a ratio scale such as 1:50 000, shown by entering the correct distance in km.

standard.source: https://www.thecorestandards.org/Math/Content/7/G/ (read live on 2026-11-11: solve problems involving scale drawings, including computing actual lengths from a scale drawing).

why: Your hiking map is drawn at 1:50 000, and the trail is 7 cm long on the map. How far is the real walk, and is it a stroll or an all-day climb?
useElsewhere: Math: ratios and proportional reasoning
Physics: scale models and drawings
Economics: unit price (price per kilo scales the same way)

objective: After this, a child in 10-18 can solve time = distance / speed for a planned route, including rearranging it to find the speed or the distance, shown by the correct time on a clock and the correct departure time.

standard.source: https://www.thecorestandards.org/Math/Content/6/RP/ (read live on 2026-11-11: solve unit rate problems including those involving unit pricing and constant speed).

why: A friend's train arrives at 3:40 pm, and you live 90 km away. If you ride at a steady 15 km/h, how long is the ride, and when must you leave?
useElsewhere: Physics: speed, velocity and motion graphs
Economics: price x quantity, cost of a trip
Environment: fuel used per trip

objective: After this, a child in 10-18 can choose between a short slow road and a long fast road by computing both travel times, shown by the correct choice and both times.
why: The mountain pass is 60 km, and you ride it at 20 km/h. The valley road is 90 km, and you ride it at 60 km/h. Which road gets you home first?
useElsewhere: Math: comparing two linear rates
Physics: average speed over several legs
Economics: toll roads and fuel costs versus time saved

objective: After this, a child in 10-18 can find the compass bearing from one place to another and split a trip into its north-south and east-west parts using sine and cosine, shown by the correct bearing and the two component distances.

standard.source: https://learning.ccsso.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/ADA-Compliant-Math-Standards.pdf (the same live read the general-knowledge tower-angle row cites).

why: A pilot must say which way to turn to reach an island 200 km away. Saying "somewhere that way" is not enough for a plan.
useElsewhere: Math: right triangles, sine and cosine
Physics: splitting a force or velocity into parts
Everyday life: setting a safe ladder angle or ramp slope

objective: After this, an adult learner can explain why the shortest flight between two far-apart places looks curved on a flat map, shown by comparing a great-circle distance with a straight line drawn on a flat map and choosing the shorter.
why: A flight from one continent to another takes a path that bends toward the pole on the wall map. Surely a straight line is shorter?
useElsewhere: Math: geometry on a sphere
Physics: why shortest paths on curved surfaces differ from flat ones
Economics: fuel cost of long-haul routes

objective: After this, a child in 7-10 can compare two distances on a map by eye and with the scale bar, shown by tapping the farther of two places from a start point and then checking with the bar.
why: You get to choose a picnic spot: the lake or the hill. Which one is the shorter walk from home?
useElsewhere: Math: estimating and comparing lengths
Everyday life: choosing the closest shop

objective: After this, a child in 10-18 can work out the clock-time difference between two places from their positions east or west of each other, shown by the correct local time at the second place.
why: Your cousin lives 6 time zones east of you. When it is 8 pm where you are, what time is it where your cousin lives?
useElsewhere: Math: addition and subtraction with a 24-hour cycle
Physics: Earth turns 15 degrees every hour (360 / 24)
Economics: when markets and shops open across the world

objective: After this, an adult learner can compare the total cost of two routes by combining distance, fuel use, a fare or toll and time, shown by the correct cheaper option and the cost difference.
why: A delivery van can take the toll road or the free road. The toll saves an hour, but is an hour worth the fee and the fuel?
useElsewhere: Economics: break-even and comparing costs
Math: linear models with two variables
Environment: fuel use per route
